competition_series: FSAE Michigan (Electric class, EV since 2023); no FS Germany or other driverless-class series entries found
summary: Cornell Racing is one of the most decorated combustion-era FSAE teams in North America (nine FSAE Michigan world championships since 1979, Rookie of the Year 1987, and a program dating to at least 1986), but it is a comparatively late and still-narrow adopter of electrification: its first-ever all-electric competition entry, ARG23, debuted at the Toyota Green Grand Prix at Watkins Glen on April 14, 2023, and its FSAE Michigan Electric-class debut followed in the same year. As of this research (September 2026), there is no public evidence that Cornell Racing has a driverless/autonomous vehicle subteam, has entered any Formula Student or FSAE Driverless-class event, or has announced an intent to participate in the new FSAE Driverless Class introduced for 2026. The team's current car (ARG26) is described purely in terms of chassis, aero, powertrain, and dynamics improvements with no autonomous features mentioned. This is reported as a genuine negative result: Cornell Racing appears to be an FSAE peer team that has NOT ramped driverless, in contrast to teams like UTFR (Toronto). Note that Cornell hosts other autonomous-vehicle-adjacent student groups (Cornell Electric Vehicles, an unrelated Shell Eco-Marathon-focused team founded 2014; and unaffiliated Cornell-adjacent academic autonomous racing research) that should not be confused with Cornell Racing's FSAE program.

recommended_sequence: N/A - not applicable in the sense of a driverless build sequence, since none exists to synthesize from. The one transferable sequencing signal from Cornell's own history is on the EV side: the team treated 'become competitive on a new powertrain architecture' (combustion to EV, 2022-2023; then single-motor EV to 4WD EV, 2025-2026) as a multi-year, one-platform-change-at-a-time process, never layering a second major architecture change (such as driverless) onto an already-in-flux platform - which is itself an implicit argument for sequencing driverless only after a platform is stable, matching the general pattern also seen in UTFR's case.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: Low direct applicability as a technical case study, since Cornell Racing has not built a driverless system - there is no EBS design, sensor suite, software stack, or timeline to copy. Its value to this study is as an honest negative data point: a top-tier, well-funded North American FSAE team with nine world championships and a 100+-person program has NOT entered the FSAE Driverless Class as of September 2026, despite the class being open since its introduction. This suggests driverless entry is not simply a function of team size, funding, or engineering pedigree, and that even strong programs may rationally choose to defer driverless investment while consolidating gains on a recent platform change (EV since 2023, 4WD since 2026). For a Winnipeg team with an existing running EV and a dedicated ~9-person software-focused DV group already committed to a 24-month driverless ramp (unlike Cornell, which has made no such commitment), the main lesson is a caution rather than a template: confirm the driverless commitment does not collide with a concurrent major base-vehicle platform change, since Cornell's own pattern suggests successful teams treat major powertrain/platform changes and driverless entry as sequential, not simultaneous, undertakings.
